newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-France, Germany launch EU reform initiative.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-France, Germany launch EU reform initiative.

text.p: France and Germany outlined joint proposals for reforming the European Union on Monday calling for closer cooperation on internal and external security and a shakeup of EU institutions.

But a joint letter by President Jacques Chirac and Chancellor Helmut Kohl to fellow EU leaders ahead of Friday's summit in Dublin left key issues vague, with two options for the appointment of a European foreign policy representative and no clear areas for the extension of majority voting.

Kohl and Chirac said their aim was to push forward slow-moving negotiations in the EU's Intergovernmental Conference (IGC) by focusing on "urgent questions" to enable the conclusion of a new treaty by June next year.

"We consider the areas of internal and external security as well as institutional reform are particularly relevant. If we do not achieve joint decisions in these areas, we will expose the whole construction of Europe to great danger and we will not meet our responsibility towards future generations," they said.

The aim is to make EU institutions more effective to cope with the expected entry of former communist central and east European countries in the coming decade, enlarging the Union eventually to up to 27 states.
French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette complained last Friday that a draft treaty produced by Ireland reflected the "mediocrity" of the IGC negotiations so far.

The 10-page letter, addressed to the EU's Irish presidency, called for new institutions to "reinforce the effectiveness, continuity, coherence, solidarity and visibility" of a common European foreign and security policy.

Under the plan, a foreign policy analysis and planning unit in Brussels would prepare joint actions, headed by a senior official "possessing the necessary political stature" who would represent EU foreign policy when joint actions were agreed.

But reflecting differences between Paris and Bonn, the letter offered two alternatives: appointing a full-time "Mr Foreign Policy", as sought by France, or giving the job to the secretary-general of the EU's Council of Ministers -- a little-known German bureaucrat.
While unanimity would remain the rule for setting foreign policy objectives at summit level, the implementation of such actions should be decided by qualified majority voting, the leaders said.

They proposed a "constructive abstention" system enabling member states to express their reservations about a decision without blocking it, and a "solidarity clause" committing them not to undermine joint foreign policy actions.

The Franco-German letter called for gradually bringing the Western European Union defence grouping under the European Union, so that EU summits could give it policy guidelines -- a move opposed by Britain.

Kohl and Chirac also proposed the creation of a "European judicial area" through a gradual harmonisation of drugs and crime legislation, the development of the Europol police agency and a gradual move to qualified majority voting on internal security issues.

They advocated a common policy on admission at external borders, visas, immigration and political asylum, as well as enhanced customs cooperation. They also demanded a harmonisation of drugs legislation -- anathema to the Netherlands -- and firmer action to fight fraud on the EU budget.
But they were vague about which areas of justice and police matters should be subject to the full European Union institutional process and when.
The leaders called for a reform of the weighted voting system "to guarantee a representative balance of member states" but gave no details.
They said the number of European commissioners must be reduced and national parliaments more closely associated with EU decision-making.
